content:
Elon Musk has said he regrets spending nearly half a billion dollars backing Republican candidates in the 2026 United States midterm elections, telling the New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday that he felt "pretty foolish" after the party lost control of both chambers of Congress.

"I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it," Musk said, speaking virtually to the summit's interviewer, Andrew Ross Sorkin. "Probably, if I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money."

The admission is striking not only for its candour but for its scale. According to the BBC, Musk contributed about $446 million to Republican campaigns during the midterm cycle, making him the largest individual political donor in American history. Campaign finance watchdog OpenSecrets put the figure at more than $445 million, while a Washington Post analysis of campaign-finance records found his total was nearly $300 million more than the next largest Republican donors, Richard and Elizabeth Uihlein.

The money flowed through a network of political action committees and Republican-aligned organisations, including America PAC, which Musk founded, the Senate Leadership Fund and the Congressional Leadership Fund. The [Economic Times reported](https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/world/us/from-im-dark-maga-to-not-maga-elon-musk-feels-pretty-foolish-spending-446-million-on-republicans-in-the-midterms/articleshow/135977739.cms), citing the BBC, that the spending made Musk the biggest individual donor in the 2026 elections, yet it could not prevent a Democratic sweep. Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate, and are due to take their majorities when the new Congress convenes in January 2027, with a 56 to 44 majority in the Senate, according to reports of the results.

The losses were sharpest in Texas, where Musk has based himself and several of his companies. He spent more than $150 million supporting Republican candidates in the state, including at least $45 million backing Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton, who lost to Democrat James Talarico in what was the Democrats' first statewide victory in Texas in more than 30 years. According to Bloomberg, two super PACs Musk funded — America PAC and Texas PAC — spent heavily on candidates who lost, and Paxton's unsuccessful bid alone drew some $229 million of the money Musk's network deployed.

Democrat Gina Hinojosa also defeated Republican Greg Abbott in the Texas governor's race, a result that underlined how far the night went against the party Musk had bankrolled. Musk acknowledged that Republican candidates might have performed even worse without his financial backing, but said the results showed that money alone could not determine an election. "It certainly shows that American elections are not just about money," he said.

What most of the early coverage of his remarks missed is the pattern behind them. This is not the first time Musk has promised to step back from political spending. In May 2025, after tens of millions of dollars he spent on a Wisconsin Supreme Court race went for nothing, he said he would spend "a lot less" on politics. That pledge did not hold: within months he was back, dropping hundreds of millions to help President Donald Trump and his Republican allies in the midterms. The DealBook remarks are therefore less a sudden change of heart than the second act of a cycle — a big bet, a public retreat, and then a bigger bet still.

Musk also used the appearance to distance himself from the movement he helped fund. "I'm not MAGA," he told the summit, adding that he was "ideologically quite moderate" and did not subscribe to "blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party." It was a remarkable statement from a man who stood on the front row at Trump's second inauguration and whose money was central to the Republican effort this autumn. [CNN noted](https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/19/politics/elon-musk-not-maga-trump?cid=external-feeds_iluminar_meta) that the turn comes after a midterm thrashing in which the world's richest man had backed the losing side with the largest personal fortune ever deployed in an American election.

The timing matters for another reason. Musk spoke on the same day that Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin met in Shenzhen for a rare trilateral summit, as [Global Wire reported](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/xi-trump-putin-summit-shenzhen-november-19), a reminder that the politics Musk is stepping back from is the same politics reshaping the world's great-power relationships. His distancing may also be commercial: Tesla and SpaceX depend on government contracts, regulatory goodwill and a customer base that spans the political spectrum, and a billionaire seen as a partisan financier carries a cost in all three.

Musk stopped short of saying he would withdraw from politics altogether, and his comments suggested he was reassessing how much he should commit to future campaigns rather than quitting them. He also signalled that his business interests remain intertwined with the artificial intelligence race, indicating that Anthropic could seek an additional 10 gigawatts of computing capacity from SpaceX — a deal that would tie the world's richest man to the company whose record-breaking public debut has dominated the markets this week.

The scale of the experiment he has just run is worth stating plainly. No individual has ever spent this much of their own money on an American election and lost this comprehensively. Buffett's $5.47 billion donation to his family foundations this week, as [Global Wire reported](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/warren-buffett-5-47-billion-berkshire-donation-november-2026), was philanthropy of a similar order of magnitude — but Musk's $446 million was a political wager, and the return on it was a Democratic Congress, a Democratic governor of Texas and a Democratic senator-elect in the state where his companies are headquartered.

Whether the regret lasts is the open question. Musk has promised to spend less before and then spent more. What is different this time is the size of the loss and the public nature of the admission, made on one of the most watched stages in American business. If he does pull back, the Republican Party will have to replace the largest single source of money it has ever had. If he does not, the next election will test again whether the richest man in the world can buy the outcome he wants — and whether, as he put it on Wednesday, American elections are really not just about money.
summary: Elon Musk has said he feels "pretty foolish" after spending about $446 million backing Republicans in the 2026 US midterms, telling the New York Times DealBook Summit he would have spent less — as Democrats took both chambers of Congress and won in Texas.
title: Elon Musk says he feels 'pretty foolish' after spending $446 million on Republicans in midterm rout
